messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  (none)

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  (none)

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

John, a 29-year-old European American man and Coast Guard officer, has been struggling with vivid yet fragmented memories following a traumatic mugging incident. It was a dark night when he was ambushed by an assailant in the narrow alley behind his apartment building. The assailant demanded John’s wallet and watch while brandishing a knife. Despite his training and usual composure, John felt utterly helpless as he watched the assailant flee with his belongings. Since that eventful night, John has found it incredibly difficult to put what happened into words. He feels like there is a chasm between him and those moments, as if trying to grasp smoke with his bare hands. The memory fragments he does have are disjointed pieces of the larger puzzle, making it hard for him to construct a coherent narrative of the event. Sometimes, John can recall specific details—the sharp blade glinting in the dim light, the panic in his chest—but they feel disconnected from each other, like scattered remnants of a shattered vase. The emotional numbness he experiences when recalling these fragments adds another layer of complexity. At times, he can vividly remember certain moments, but it feels as though someone else was there instead of him. This detachment leaves John feeling isolated and confused about his own reactions to the trauma. He often finds himself staring blankly at a screen or out the window, trying to piece together what happened, only to feel more frustrated with each attempt. John’s relationship with his partner has been strained as he struggles to share these fragmented memories. His inability to articulate his experiences leaves him feeling distant and disconnected from her. She notices that John seems less engaged in their conversations about everyday events and often retreats into silence when she tries to talk about the mugging. This emotional distance is painful for both of them, and it has created a sense of unease between them. John’s work as a Coast Guard officer requires him to be vigilant and ready for any situation, but his fragmented memories make that increasingly difficult. He finds himself second-guessing his own responses in high-stress situations at work, which can affect his performance. The disjointed nature of his recollections makes it hard for him to trust his judgment and instincts. What frightens John most is the possibility that he might forget critical details forever or that these fragments will always remain disconnected, leaving him unable to fully understand what happened. He has come to believe that if he could just piece together a complete picture, he would be able to move on from this trauma. However, each attempt at recall only serves to reinforce his feelings of numbness and detachment. It is this growing sense of isolation and the fear that he will never truly process or understand what happened that has finally brought John to seek help. He hopes for a way to integrate these memories so they no longer feel like separate, unconnected pieces. His goal is to find a way to reconnect with both his past and present, and to reclaim some sense of emotional coherence in the face of this trauma.
